rh-l2prae.summary: Brief preamble to Book II. After a rubric attributing the questions to Holcot, it connects Lombard's account of man's creation for the service and enjoyment of God with the end of Book I on predestination and foreknowledge, motivating the first question on God's just governance of humankind.
claims: Book II opens by continuing Book I's theme of divine governance of rational creatures.

rh-l2prae-d1e100.summary: Editorial rubric opening the questions on Book II of the Sentences, attributed to 'master Robert Holcot, a man most subtle', and introducing a preliminary remark.

rh-l2prae-d1e118.summary: Links Book II to Book I. Lombard's first distinction of Book II treats the creation of man, made to serve and enjoy God, while the end of Book I treats God's governance of rational creatures through predestination and foreknowledge. Joining the two, Holcot introduces his first question, on whether God justly governs the human race.
claims: Book II's treatment of creation continues Book I's treatment of divine governance through predestination and foreknowledge.
Man was created to serve and enjoy God.
